thread.title: Hewlett-Packard (HPQ) 3rd Quarter Earnings: What to Expect

author: Richard Saintvilus
title: Hewlett-Packard (HPQ) 3rd Quarter Earnings: What to Expect
text:
Shutterstock photo Can Hewlett-Packard ( HPQ ) maintain its winning streak?
The global PC manufacturer is trading at near five-year highs and has seen its share price rise 10% just over the past thirty days. It would seem investors are betting on strong results and a sustained momentum when the company reports third quarter fiscal 2018 earnings results after Thursday’s closing bell.
For the quarter that ended July, the Palo Alto, Calif.-based company is expected to earn 51 cents per share on revenue of $14.26 billion. This compares to the year-ago quarter when earnings came to 43 cents per share on revenue of $13.06 billion. For the full year, ending in October, earnings are projected to increase 20% year over year to $1.97 per share, while revenue of $57.64 billion would mark a 10.7% year-over-year rise.
While the company has delivered seven straight quarters of revenue growth, investors aren’t willing to forget the suffering they’ve been through due to multiple quarters of declines since 2010. But thanks to the recent revival in worldwide PC sales, which in the second quarter grew for the first time in six years, HP’s outlook has gotten brighter. Worldwide PC shipments rose 1.4% year over year to 62.1 million units in the second quarter, according to research firm Gartner.
This growth rate bodes well for HP, which is now a formidable competitor to Apple ( AAPL ) among PC sales. Last quarter the company enjoyed a 14% rise in its personal systems revenues, thanks to a 7% jump in total units sold. The company, which has averaged double-digit top-line growth in five straight quarters, has performed much better than Wall Street expected since splitting from Hewlett Packard Enterprise ( HPE ) in November 2015.
And Thursday’s results should mirror the growth rate HP has delivered in recent quarters, particularly given not only the strength in consumer spending, but also increased demand consumers have shown for higher-end personal computing models. Elsewhere, analysts will want to see continued strength in the company’s printing segment, which last quarter enjoyed 11% rise in revenue, driven by a 13% rise in unit sales.
The company’s decision to grow its capabilities in the high-end printer market has been wise move, especially since that market also generates sales of high-margin accessories and supplies. On Thursday Wall Street will want to see the extent to which HP can continue to capitalize on the industry’s revival and show enough growth in the printing segment (or margin) to make these shares — currently near 52-week highs — a compelling investment today.
All told, HP is not going to excite growth investors and the company’s share price is trading too rich to appeal to value investors. But the company does pay a solid dividend that yields 2.27% annually, which — when combined with the growth in the PC market — is solid enough to buy time and allow the management to execute on its stated objectives of returning value to shareholders.
